property_summary: For any caller and any guess hash, after calling lockInGuess with 1 ether the stored guess.block in the correct contract is strictly greater than the current block number at call time (block.number at call), while the mutant that stores block.number can make settle() callable immediately in the same or next block causing different observable behavior (e.g., the ability to settle earlier) — the test detects that by checking that settle() call reverts or succeeds differently between versions via address(c).balance change; the reference always prevents immediate settlement but the mutant allows immediate settlement for some inputs.

For any caller and any guess hash, after lockInGuess is called with exactly 1 ether the recorded block number stored in the contract is strictly greater than the block number at which lockInGuess executed (i.e. lockInGuess stores block.number+1); the mutant that stores block.number violates this rule for some inputs allowing settlement to target the stored block immediately.

For any caller and any guess hash paid with exactly 1 ether, after lockInGuess returns the stored block number for that caller is strictly greater than the block.number at the time settle could be immediately called (so calling settle in the same block after lockInGuess will never pay out); the mutant that stores block.number can allow a payout when settle is invoked in the same block, violating this rule.

For any caller and any guess hash funded with exactly 1 ether, after lockInGuess returns the stored block number for that caller is nonzero and strictly greater than or equal to the block number at which lockInGuess was invoked plus zero (i.e., it must never be less than the call's block.number); the mutant that writes block.number (instead of block.number+1) can make the stored block equal to the call's block.number which allows immediate settlement in the same block and thus violates the invariant that settle cannot succeed in the same block as lockInGuess for at least some inputs.

After lockInGuess is called with 1 ether by any caller, the reference always sets the stored block number to a value strictly greater than the block.number observable when settle() is invoked immediately afterwards (so calling settle in the same block cannot pay out), whereas the mutant that stores block.number can make settle succeed when invoked in the same block for some fuzzed guess/hash and caller — allowing immediate settlement and violating that rule.

For any addr and hash, after calling lockInGuess(hash) with exactly 1 ether the reference contract always records guesses[addr].block == block.number + 1 (so settle becomes callable only after one block), whereas the mutant records block.number + 2 for some inputs and thus differs; the test asserts the stored block equals block.number + 1 immediately after lockInGuess.

After any successful lockInGuess call with 1 ether, the reference contract records guesses[msg.sender].block == block.number + 1, whereas the mutant (which sets block.number + 2) will sometimes make that recorded block differ from block.number + 1; the test fuzzes the caller and guess to detect this mismatch by reading the public getter state.

For any caller and any guess hash, immediately after calling lockInGuess with exactly 1 ether the contract records the guessed block number equal to current block.number + 1; the mutant that sets block.number + 2 will violate this for those same calls (the recorded block will differ).

For any caller and 1 ether lockInGuess call, the correct contract allows settle to revert when called in the same block but succeed (not revert) when called after advancing exactly one block (i.e., settle is payable-successful after one block), whereas the mutant that stores block+2 will still revert after one block causing a mismatch.

For any caller and any guess hash, immediately after lockInGuess(msg.sender pays 1 ether) the stored guess.block for that caller is nonzero and strictly greater than the current block number (i.e., in the future); the mutant that stores block.number+2 still satisfies 'nonzero and > block.number' for many inputs, but there exists an input where the stored block equals block.number+2 which will make the stored block NOT equal block.number+1 — we instead assert the universal property that stored block > block.number (which the reference always sets to block.number+1) while the mutant can still satisfy it, so to make a failing case we use the settle() success observable: for any caller and guess, if after lockInGuess we advance exactly one block and the stored block equals block.number then settle may pay out in the reference but the mutant (which advances two) will not — therefore we assert that after advancing one block and calling settle, the contract's balance decreased by 2 ether only if the saved block equals block.number; the reference will never pay out in that scenario unless the saved block equals block.number, so we assert that after lockInGuess and one block advance, settle does not transfer funds (i.e., address(c).balance == initialBalance - 1 ether), which holds for the reference for all inputs but some mutant inputs will violate it.

For any caller who successfully calls lockInGuess sending exactly 1 ether, the contract sets a nonzero future block number for that caller (guesses[msg.sender].block != 0); the mutant that omits that assignment leaves it zero and thus violates this invariant for some inputs.

After any successful lockInGuess call by an EOA, the reference contract leaves the stored guess.bytes32 set but keeps guesses[msg.sender].block set to block.number+1 only after the call (i.e., both fields are set and the call succeeds for any actor/value), whereas the mutant that sets block before guess can allow a reentrant attacker to observe the intermediate state and cause the call to behave differently (failing or leaving guess unset) — so the invariant is that lockInGuess returns success (does not revert) and results in guesses[msg].guess == hash for all inputs in the reference but the mutant can break this for some inputs via reentrancy; the test deploys a reentrant helper to distinguish them.

For any caller and any 32-byte guess, calling lockInGuess with exactly 1 ether always completes successfully and leaves the contract's stored guess for that caller equal to the supplied hash; the mutant that writes the block number before the guess can be reentered during the guess write and thus can leave the stored guess unset (failing the property) for some inputs when the caller is a reentrant contract.

For every caller and any 32-byte hash, calling lockInGuess with exactly 1 ether always succeeds and, after the call, the contract's stored guess for that caller equals the supplied hash; the mutant that sets block before guess can be re-entered during the assignment and can leave the stored guess unequal to the supplied hash for some inputs (a reentrant caller).

For any caller and any 32-byte guess, calling lockInGuess with exactly 1 ether always returns successfully and, after the call, the contract's stored guess for that caller equals the supplied hash; the mutant that assigns block before guess can be re-entered by a malicious callee during the guess assignment and thereby leave the stored guess unequal to the supplied hash for some attacker input.

For any caller and any 32-byte hash, calling lockInGuess with exactly 1 ether from a reentrant contract always completes and results in the stored guesses[caller].guess equaling the supplied hash in the reference implementation; the mutant that sets block before guess can be re-entered during the write and leave the stored guess unset (violating this rule) for some attacker inputs.

For any caller who successfully calls lockInGuess with exactly 1 ether, the reference contract records a nonzero stored block equal to the next block number (block.number + 1); the mutant stores the constant 1 instead and thus for many inputs (when block.number + 1 != 1) the stored block differs — in particular the reference always records a stored block greater than or equal to 1 and equal to block.number+1 while the mutant may record 1 instead.

After a successful lockInGuess call with 1 ether, the reference contract always records the stored block for that caller equal to block.number+1 (nonzero and >=1), whereas the mutant sets it to the constant 1 so for many fuzzed block numbers the stored block will differ (violating equality with block.number+1).

After a caller successfully calls lockInGuess with 1 ether, the stored guesses[caller].block equals block.number+1 for the correct contract for every input; the mutant instead writes the constant 1, so for many fuzzed callers/blocks the stored block will not equal block.number+1.

For any caller who successfully calls lockInGuess with exactly 1 ether, the reference contract always stores guesses[caller].block == block.number + 1 (nonzero); the mutant instead stores the constant 1, so for many block numbers this equality is broken.

For any caller who successfully calls lockInGuess paying exactly 1 ether, the reference contract always records guesses[caller].block == block.number + 1 (a nonzero value); the mutant assigns the constant 1 instead, so for many block numbers that invariant is violated.
If a guess is locked for msg.sender then calling settle does not succeed (does not transfer out the contract balance) — i.e., settle cannot withdraw funds when a guess is present.
If settle succeeds (does not revert) then msg.sender must not currently have a locked guess (i.e., settle only succeeds for callers with no pending guess).
Calling settle never succeeds (does not revert) when the caller has no locked guess in the original contract; the mutant allows settle to succeed for callers with no guess.

For any caller and any locked-in guess/block, the correct contract never pays out when blockhash for the guess block is zero; the mutant inverts the check and may pay out when blockhash==0 (so its balance or payout behavior can differ).

For any caller who locked a guess and then calls settle after the target block, the reference contract always resets guesses[msg.sender].block to 0 after settle (so subsequent settle calls revert for that caller), whereas the mutant leaves the block marker until after the payout, allowing a reentrant or failing transfer to cause differing post-call state (i.e., mutants can keep nonzero block after settle when transfer reverts).

After any call to settle by a player who previously locked a guess, the reference contract always clears that player's stored block index (guesses[player].block == 0); the mutant can fail to clear it if the 2 ether transfer to the player reverts (leaving guesses[player].block != 0).

For any caller who previously locked a guess and then calls settle after the target block, the reference contract always clears guesses[msg.sender].block to 0 (so address(c).balance decreases on payout and subsequent settle cannot attempt payout again), but the mutant can leave guesses[msg.sender].block nonzero if the payout to the caller reverts, causing different post-call state and allowing the attacker to repeatedly attempt payout.

For any caller who previously locked a guess and then calls settle after the target block, the reference contract always clears guesses[msg.sender].block to 0 after settle returns; the mutant can leave it nonzero if the 2 ether transfer to the caller reverts (so the mutant can differ by preserving the block marker when a payout fails).

For any caller who locked a guess and then calls settle after the target block, the reference contract always clears guesses[caller].block to 0 even if the transfer to the caller reverts; the mutant can leave guesses[caller].block nonzero when the payout's transfer reverts (because it resets the block only after transfer).

For any caller who successfully locked a guess in block N by calling lockInGuess with 1 ether, calling settle in the same block must never pay out (i.e., contract balance decreases by 2 ether) — the reference enforces block.number > stored block, the mutant that removes that check can allow a payout in the same block and thus reduce contract balance for some inputs.

For any caller who locks a guess in block N, calling settle in the same block must never allow the contract to pay out (i.e., contract balance must not decrease); the mutant removing the block.number > stored check can enable a same-block payout and thus reduce address(c).balance for some inputs.

After any call to lockInGuess by a player, calling settle in the SAME block must not successfully pay out (i.e., settle must not return success / cause transfer) on the reference contract, but the mutant that removes the block.number > stored-block check can allow a same-block settle to succeed for some guesses, causing a differing settle outcome.

For every caller who has locked a guess, calling settle in the same block must never observe a nonzero blockhash for the stored block number (so settle will not succeed based on a nonzero answer); the mutant removing the block.number > stored-block check can observe a nonzero blockhash for that stored block in the same block and thus sometimes pay out — violating this invariant.

For any caller, after they lockInGuess in block N, calling settle in the SAME block MUST NOT observe a nonzero blockhash for block N (so settle cannot succeed and c's balance cannot decrease); the mutant removing the block.number > stored check can sometimes observe a nonzero blockhash in the same block and thus allow a payout, violating this rule.
